stem: During electrosurgery, why should local surgical-smoke evacuation remain active whenever smoke is produced?

options.A: To replace the need for general room ventilation during electrosurgery.
options.B: To remove surgical smoke only after it has dispersed into the room air.
options.C: To capture hazardous airborne contaminants close to their source before they disperse.
options.D: To prevent the electrosurgical unit from interfering with physiologic monitoring equipment.

rationale: NIOSH states that electrosurgical smoke can contain toxic gases and vapors, bioaerosols, cellular material, and viruses. General room ventilation alone is not sufficient to capture contaminants generated at the source; local exhaust ventilation such as a smoke evacuator is used to control the plume close to the surgical site, and the evacuator should be activated whenever airborne particles are produced. Therefore C is correct. A incorrectly treats local evacuation as a replacement for general ventilation, B waits until contaminants have dispersed rather than capturing them at the source, and D describes a purpose unrelated to surgical-smoke control.
educational_objective: Use local surgical-smoke evacuation during electrosurgical plume generation to capture hazardous airborne contaminants close to their source before they disperse into the room.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) / National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
source_document_title: NIOSH Hazard Controls HC11 — Control of Smoke from Laser/Electric Surgical Procedures
source_version_date: DHHS (NIOSH) Publication No. 96-128, September 1996; permanent CDC Stacks record and current NIOSH linkage rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: CDC Stacks record description, corresponding to HC11 Hazard/Controls sections: surgical smoke may contain toxic gases and vapors, bioaerosols, cellular material, and viruses; general room ventilation is insufficient; local smoke evacuation captures contaminants near the source; the evacuator should be activated whenever airborne particles are produced. Currentness cross-check: NIOSH Healthcare Respiratory Protection > Surgical smoke (Jan. 15, 2025) directs use of control methods such as ventilation and links this NIOSH publication.
source_claim_supported: Local surgical-smoke evacuation is an engineering control used to capture hazardous airborne contaminants close to the source and should be active whenever surgical procedures generate airborne particles.

source_original.stem: During electrosurgery, why should local surgical-smoke evacuation remain active whenever smoke is produced?

options.A: To lower ambient room temperature around the surgical field.
options.B: To reduce the time required to complete electrosurgical procedures.
options.C: To capture hazardous smoke particles, gases, and vapors close to the source.
options.D: To prevent electrosurgical equipment from interfering with physiologic monitors.

source_original.rationale: NIOSH recommends local exhaust control because surgical smoke can contain hazardous gases, vapors, particles, bioaerosols, and cellular material. Option C states the infection/occupational-safety purpose. The other choices are not the function of surgical-smoke evacuation.
source_original.source_detail: NIOSH Hazard Controls HC11: surgical smoke can contain toxic gases, vapors, bioaerosols and cellular material; local exhaust ventilation/smoke evacuation should capture smoke close to its source and remain active whenever airborne particles are produced. DHHS (NIOSH) Publication 96-128; page last reviewed 2014 and recommendation remains referenced by current NIOSH surgical-smoke guidance; live currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: transmission precautions, PPE, device/environmental safety, asepsis, identification and infection-prevention activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the stem and key C. Replaced the obsolete/broken final source URL with the permanent CDC Stacks record, cross-checked current NIOSH surgical-smoke guidance that still links HC11, and rewrote distractors to test realistic misunderstandings about engineering controls rather than unrelated room temperature or procedure-speed claims.

audit_findings.source_authority: NIOSH/CDC primary occupational-safety guidance; NCSBN 2026 for blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: HC11 is a 1996 NIOSH publication preserved in CDC Stacks; current NIOSH Healthcare Respiratory Protection guidance dated 2025-01-15 still directs ventilation controls for surgical smoke and links HC11; rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: CDC Stacks HC11 description/Controls and Work Practices; NIOSH Healthcare Respiratory Protection > Surgical smoke
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses directly supported claims only: surgical plume contains hazardous airborne contaminants, general room ventilation alone is insufficient, LEV captures near source, and evacuation remains active while airborne particles are generated. No unsupported exposure threshold is added.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because NIOSH recommends a combination of general and local exhaust ventilation; LEV does not replace all general ventilation.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because source capture is intended before plume disperses into room air.
distractor_audit.D: Electromagnetic interference prevention is not the stated function of smoke evacuation.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C describes the engineering-control purpose and source-capture principle supported by NIOSH.
audit_findings.cueing: All options describe operational purposes of the smoke-control setup; correct-answer wording is not copied verbatim from the stem.
audit_findings.blueprint: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — environmental/occupational hazard control during procedures.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-audited currentness, permanent source record, NIOSH current linkage, stem, each distractor, key, rationale, objective, NCSBN mapping, ambiguity and cueing from zero. C remained uniquely correct.
